story_type: remote-controlled airliner deliberately crashed in a safety test, fireball and cabin cameras
hook: No crew aboard. NASA crashed this jetliner on purpose.
narration: There was no crew aboard this airliner when it hit the desert floor.
On December first, nineteen eighty four, NASA and the FAA crashed a Boeing 720 on purpose at Edwards Air Force Base.
A NASA research pilot flew it by remote control from a console on the ground.
Its tanks held seventy six thousand pounds of fuel, blended with an additive meant to stop a crash fire.
Treated fuel stays in heavy drops instead of a fine mist, and that mist is what ignites after a crash.
The plan was a wings level belly landing, with eight steel posts slicing open the wing tanks.
Then the left wing dropped and hit the lakebed first, short of the cutters.
The jet skidded sideways, and a cutter tore into an engine on the right wing.
The fuel burst into a massive fireball.
The right wing broke off and folded over as the fire swallowed the fuselage.
Inside, cameras showed the dummies being shaken, while the seats stayed attached to the floor.
The fire took more than an hour to put out.
outcome: The additive failed to slow the fire, and the crash data helped the FAA set new fire safety rules for airliners.
title: NASA crashed a jetliner on purpose
description:
On Dec. 1, 1984, NASA and the FAA crashed a remotely piloted Boeing 720 onto Rogers Dry Lake at Edwards Air Force Base to test a fire-suppressing fuel additive and new cabin safety features.

facts.claim: NASA and the FAA intentionally crashed a remotely controlled Boeing 720
facts.source_quote: a joint project between NASA and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that intentionally crashed a remotely controlled Boeing 720 aircraft

facts.claim: The crash was on Dec. 1, 1984 at Rogers Dry Lake, Edwards AFB, into steel structures meant to rip open the wing tanks
facts.source_quote: an intentional crash-landing of the remotely piloted aircraft into several steel structures set up on Rogers Dry Lake at Edwards Air Force Base to rip open wing fuel tanks.

facts.claim: Flown from a ground console, 76,000 pounds of modified fuel
facts.source_quote: The fuel tanks were filled with 76,000 pounds of the modified Jet-A fuel and all engines ran normally from start-up to impact during the nine-minute flight.

facts.claim: Left wing hit first, cutter struck the right inboard engine, fireball, right wing broke off, fire over an hour
facts.source_quote: its left wing dropped and contacted the ground first, short of the wing cutters. This caused the nose of the airliner to swing to the left as it skidded on the lakebed surface at about a 45-degree angle. As a result, one wing cutter struck the inboard engine on the right wing, destroying the engine and causing a massive fuel leak that immediately burst into flame.

facts.claim: Dummies shaken, seats stayed attached; additive ineffective; data helped FAA set new fire rules
facts.source_quote: Cameras inside the airliner showed crash dummies being shaken and small panels falling during the crash-landing, although the seats remained attached to the floor.

extra_sources.excerpt: The flight plan called for the aircraft to touch down wheels-up on a specially prepared runway on the east side of the dry lakebed with its wings level and exactly on the center line, allowing the fuselage to remain intact as the wings were sliced open by eight steel posts cemented into the lakebed.

The airliner continued to yaw to the left until it was nearly sideways, causing the damaged right wing to break off and fold over and the fuselage to be engulfed in a massive fuel-fed fireball. The fire took more than an hour to fully extinguish.
the full-scale demonstration in a real-world flight environment showed that the modified anti-misting fuel was ineffective in reducing the propagation or intensity of fire.
Research data from the project in these areas yielded new data on impact survivability that helped the FAA establish new rules regarding fire prevention and fire-retardant materials.
During the 14 flights made with safety pilots on board, the Boeing 720 was controlled remotely by a pilot in a ground-based console for 16 hours and 22 minutes
